e.t: This Hebrew word means “fist,” naming the hand when it is clenched. It functions as a noun referring to a physical part of the body, rather than an action or quality. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Exodus 21:18 and Isaiah 58:4. Its basic meaning remains the same in both occurrences; the surrounding verse determines how that fist is involved in the sentence.

The word means “sons,” functioning as a noun for male children or members of a family line. In this Hebrew Old Testament corpus, it occurs 11 times, appearing in Ezra and Daniel. Its use can identify sons in an ordinary family setting and can also refer to people viewed within a larger family or lineage. It is therefore a relational word, naming people by their place within a family. The surrounding verse determines which relationship is intended.

This Hebrew word means “desired” and functions as a verb, describing the act or state of wanting something. It presents desire as directed toward an object or outcome rather than as a mere description of a person. The word occurs 12 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all within Daniel, from Daniel 2:13 through Daniel 7:16. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on what is being desired and the surrounding wording.

Berothah is a Hebrew place-name, referring to a location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. It is represented in English as “Berothai” and “Berothah.” This word appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 2 Samuel 8:8 and Ezekiel 47:16. The two English forms are renderings of the same Hebrew word, while the precise significance of the named location depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to spices—fragrant substances used as valuable goods, offerings, or stored provisions. It is a noun, naming the spices themselves rather than an action. The word occurs 29 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in descriptions of the tabernacle materials, royal gifts and trade, and storehouse provisions. Its use in these settings presents spices as tangible, desirable substances that could be prepared, given, received, or kept. The precise significance in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word refers to “goats,” the plural name for those animals. It functions as a noun rather than describing an action or quality. Within the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, it occurs twice, both times in the Song of Songs: Song 4:1 and Song 6:5. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding verse text, but its ordinary lexical sense is the animals themselves.

e.t: Aholibamah is a personal name, referring to a woman in the Hebrew Old Testament rather than expressing a general quality or action. The name appears eight times, chiefly in Genesis 36, where it is connected with family relationships, children, and genealogy. English Bibles render it as “Aholibamah” or “Oholibamah.” Because no short definition or lexical gloss is provided, its precise name meaning cannot be stated from this evidence alone. Its normal use is as an identifying name within genealogical records.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to “doors,” the movable entrances that provide or restrict access to a building or room. It can describe doors as physical objects in ordinary homes, palaces, and sacred places. The word occurs 89 times in the Hebrew Bible, showing regular use for architectural entrances and their opening or closing. Its wider scriptural associations also include speech, commands, and giving, where doors may serve as the object being mentioned or acted upon.

This Hebrew word is used as a connective or adverb meaning “however” or “truly.” It can mark a contrast with what has just been said, or give emphasis to the truth of a statement. It appears 19 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its precise force depends on how it links the surrounding words. Its use ranges from simple contrast to firm affirmation.

This Hebrew verb describes something flowing or pouring out. It can refer to water or other liquid moving from a source, and it is also used for bodily discharge. In the Old Testament, the word appears 42 times, with its uses especially visible in descriptions of a land flowing with abundance and in laws concerning bodily flows. Its basic picture is movement outward from one place, whether the flow is a blessing from the land or a physical discharge. The precise force in a particular verse depends on what is flowing and the surrounding sentence.

This Hebrew verb means “sow”: it describes putting seed into the ground so that it may grow and produce a crop. It is used for the practical act of planting, whether in ordinary farming or in commands about when land may be worked. The word occurs 56 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a recurring agricultural action rather than a rare or specialized idea. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

Huri is a Hebrew personal name, used to identify an individual rather than to express an action, quality, or general idea. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at 1 Chronicles 5:14, and the English renderings preserve it as “Huri.” Because no explicit lexical definition or surrounding verse text is available here, the safest meaning is the name itself: Huri. Its precise significance in that verse must come from the surrounding passage.

e.t: Hiram is a Hebrew personal name, rendered "Hiram" in English. It refers to a named individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears 26 times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, across 21 verses, especially in 1 Kings. Its repeated use in passages involving speech, giving, and relationships shows that it functions as a person’s name within the biblical narrative, while the name itself does not express a general quality or concept.

This Hebrew word refers to a pipe or flute, a musical instrument used to produce sound. It functions as a noun and appears in descriptions of musicians, celebrations, and mourning. In the Old Testament, it occurs six times, with English renderings centered on “pipes.” The word therefore identifies an instrument rather than the music itself or the people playing it. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary sense is a pipe-like wind instrument used in musical expression.

This Hebrew word refers to wine, the fermented drink mentioned in several Old Testament passages. It functions as a noun, naming a drink that could be supplied for official use or consumed at a royal feast. The word occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament: twice in Ezra and four times in Daniel. Its basic meaning remains consistent across these occurrences, while the surrounding passage determines the particular situation in which the wine appears.

This Hebrew word refers to “decrees”—formal decisions issued with authority. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in Judges 5:15 and Isaiah 10:1. In Isaiah, the word is connected with writing, presenting decrees as written decisions. Its precise force in each passage depends on the surrounding verse text, but the central idea is an authoritative decree or decision.

This Hebrew word means “the” and functions as a definite article, identifying a particular person, thing, or idea rather than speaking of one generally. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in Daniel 2:22. Its basic role is grammatical: it helps mark a noun as definite. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding Hebrew sentence and passage, but its ordinary meaning is limited to this identifying function.

The Hebrew word means “prey,” referring to what is seized by a predator or attacker. It appears once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 23:28, so its ordinary lexical meaning is clear, while its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. The word identifies what has been captured or taken, rather than the act of taking it.

This Hebrew word means “clean.” It describes something regarded as free from uncleanness or impurity. In the Old Testament, it is used for people, animals, and objects, including items associated with worship. The word occurs 94 times across 86 Old Testament verses, from Genesis through Malachi, showing that “clean” is a recurring biblical category rather than a rare or specialized term. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on what person or thing is being described there.

e.t: This Hebrew word is a personal name, rendered “Abijah.” It identifies several different people in the Old Testament rather than describing a general quality or action. The name appears 25 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in genealogies, accounts of families, and records of leaders and priests. Its role is therefore that of a proper name: the surrounding passage is needed to determine which individual named Abijah is intended.

This Hebrew word means “other,” describing someone or something as distinct from one already mentioned. It points to an additional or different person, thing, or kingdom rather than the first one under discussion. The word occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Daniel, where its normal function remains a concise way to distinguish one subject from another. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Jashen is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or command. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this word appears once, in 2 Samuel 23:32, and its English rendering is “Jashen.” Because it functions as a name, its meaning is primarily identification: it tells the reader who is being named, rather than conveying a broader idea or practice. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain that person’s specific role in the passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word functions as a personal name: “Caleb.” It refers to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both within 1 Chronicles 2:24. Its recorded setting is genealogical, and the word participates in a birth-or-begetting relationship in that passage. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its specific role there.

This Hebrew word refers to “wares,” meaning goods spoken of as items belonging to or carried by someone. It functions as a term for things, not an action or description of a person. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, in Jeremiah 10:17. Because it occurs only there and no surrounding verse text is available here, its precise force in that sentence must be understood from the passage itself. Its recorded English rendering is consistently “wares.”

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to the Chaldeans, a people repeatedly mentioned in the Old Testament. It functions as a national or people-group designation, appearing in accounts involving speech, conflict, death, and the giving of Jerusalem into their power. The word occurs 82 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Habakkuk, with especially frequent use in Jeremiah. Its central meaning remains the identification of the Chaldeans as a distinct people involved in the historical events described by the prophets and historical books.

e.t: “Lo-Ruhamah” is a personal name used in the book of Hosea. It functions as the name assigned to a person rather than as a general description used throughout the Old Testament. This name occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all within Hosea 1:6 and 1:8. Its role is connected with naming and birth in those passages, while the precise force intended there belongs to the surrounding verse and passage. The name is also rendered “Lo-Ruhamah” in one recorded English rendering.

This Hebrew verb means “swallow.” It describes the action of taking something in completely. The word appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in Job 6:3 and once in Obadiah 1:16. In both occurrences, it functions as the action being expressed in the sentence. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains the act of swallowing. It is therefore a concrete action word that may be understood from what is being swallowed and who or what performs the action.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “nothing.” It functions as an indefinite pronoun, referring broadly to the absence of an object, possession, or matter under discussion. Its exact force depends on the sentence in which it appears, but its central idea remains the lack of anything. It occurs 32 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across 32 verses, showing regular use in statements and questions about what is absent or unavailable.

The word means “anguish,” naming a painful condition a person may experience. It is a Hebrew Old Testament word found three times, in Job and Isaiah. Rather than describing an action, it identifies a condition associated with hardship and constraint. The surrounding sentence determines whose anguish is meant and how it functions there; the word itself points to the painful condition.

This Hebrew word means “deep,” referring to great depth or a profound place. In its one occurrence in the Hebrew Bible, it functions as a descriptive term for depth. The available English rendering is consistently “deep,” supporting this central sense. Its precise force in Psalm 95:4 depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context, which is not included here.

Jarkon is a Hebrew proper name used to identify a named place or feature. It is preserved as “Jarkon” in the available English rendering rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive term. The word occurs twice within the Hebrew Old Testament data, both occurrences appearing in Joshua 19:46. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise local reference cannot be described further; its basic function is to name Jarkon.

Michmethath is a Hebrew place-name, referring to a location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. It appears twice in the Old Testament, both times in Joshua, and the English rendering is consistently “Michmethath.” Because no short definition or lexical gloss is available, the safest reader-level understanding is simply this proper name for a place. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Eliel is a personal name, rendered “Eliel.” It identifies individual people in the Hebrew Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs ten times, all in genealogical or listing passages in 1 Chronicles and 2 Chronicles. Because the available passages present it as a person’s name and do not provide a short definition, its ordinary meaning here is its identifying function: Eliel names particular individuals. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding genealogy or list.

Thus, its ordinary function here is to identify an individual in a family record, while the surrounding passage supplies the specific family connection.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to something given “free”—offered willingly rather than forced or taken. In the Old Testament, it commonly describes voluntary gifts or offerings presented to God. It can also express a freely made commitment or contribution. The word occurs 26 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with its uses especially connected to giving, offerings, and willing service. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being freely given and the surrounding context.

Naam is a personal name, rendered as “Naam.” It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. This Hebrew word occurs once in the Old Testament corpus, in 1 Chronicles 4:15. The word itself supplies the individual’s name, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain that person’s family connection or role. Its meaning is therefore chiefly a name designation, not a description with a broader stated definition.

This Hebrew word expresses the action of “cast” and “up.” It describes something being thrown, placed, or raised in an upward direction or position. Its use can apply to physical movement as well as the lifting or exalting of something, depending on the sentence. The word occurs 12 times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, appearing in passages from Exodus, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and elsewhere. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word describes an action, with the meaning “deal.” It functions as a verb rather than naming a person, place, or object. The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament: once in Psalm 71:4 and once in Isaiah 26:10. Its use as a predicate presents what someone does, so the surrounding sentence determines the precise sense of the action. The available passages show that this word is uncommon and appears in two separate Old Testament verses.

This Hebrew word refers to a place named “Mishpat.” It is not presented here as an ordinary action or quality, but as a geographic name within the Old Testament account. The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Genesis 14:7, so its use is highly limited. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and account, but the word itself identifies the named place “Mishpat.”

This Hebrew word means “leaves,” referring to the foliage or leafy covering of a tree. It functions as a concrete noun naming the tree’s leaves rather than an action or quality. The word occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Daniel chapter 4. Its repeated use there confirms a consistent reference to leaves, while the surrounding verse determines the particular statement being made about them.

This Hebrew word means “surety”: it describes taking responsibility for another person or matter. It can function in statements about standing for someone, accepting an obligation, or placing something under another person’s responsibility. The word occurs 23 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages in Genesis and Psalms where a person is spoken of as surety. Its broader uses also involve people or things being joined under a shared responsibility.

This Hebrew word refers to “thoughts”—the inward mental activity of a person. It is a noun-like word describing what occupies the mind rather than an outward action. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Psalm 146:4. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and context, but its basic meaning is the mental content or considerations held within a person.

Paltiel is a Hebrew personal name used to identify a man, rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Numbers 34:26 and 2 Samuel 3:15. English renderings preserve the name as “Paltiel.” Since this is a proper name, its ordinary function is to distinguish the person being mentioned; its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse context.

e.t: The Hebrew word means “overseer.” It functions as a designation for a person entrusted with responsibility over others or an assigned task. In the Old Testament, it occurs 13 times, describing a recognized role rather than an isolated idea. Its uses include settings involving kings and organized service, showing that an overseer holds a defined place of responsibility. The precise force in any verse depends on its surrounding text.

This Hebrew word means “crooked.” It is a describing term, presenting something as crooked rather than naming an action, person, or object. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Deuteronomy 32:5. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the word’s exact force in that sentence cannot be explained further; its established lexical sense remains “crooked.”

This Hebrew word means “burn,” describing the act of burning. It functions as a verb rather than naming a person, object, or place. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 27:4, so its broader range cannot be established from repeated uses. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the available meaning points directly to burning as an action.

This Hebrew word means “things” and is used to identify what is being referred to. It appears ten times in the Old Testament, describing a broad category rather than a rare, specialized idea. Its exact force depends on the sentence in which it appears, but its ordinary function is to point to what is under discussion. It does not by itself explain the particular subject or event in any one verse.

“Kushaiah” is a personal name identifying an individual. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 15:17. Because no explicit definition is available, the safest ordinary meaning is the name itself: “Kushaiah.” It functions as a proper name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word’s lexical force is to identify a person by name.

This Hebrew word means “parched,” describing something in a dry, withered, or heat-affected condition. It functions as a descriptive word, identifying the condition of a thing rather than naming an action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs four times, so its meaning is focused and specific rather than broad. Its uses range across descriptions connected with food, bodily condition, and judgment, showing that the word can describe both physical objects and people under severe affliction.

This Hebrew word means “mock” or “mocked”: it describes treating someone or something with scorn, ridicule, or contempt. It functions as an action word, describing what people do when they deride others rather than treating them with respect. In the Old Testament, it occurs four times, in four verses, and its renderings consistently point to mocking or scoffing. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding context, but the central idea remains deliberate ridicule or scorn.

This Hebrew word means “lie,” describing the act or position of lying down. It tells what a person, animal, or other subject does or is doing. In its Old Testament usage, it occurs 30 times, so it can describe this action or state in several kinds of passages. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Hebrew word means “ways.” It functions as a noun, naming ways in connection with a person. In the Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in Daniel, and both occurrences are rendered “ways.” Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its ordinary lexical contribution is the noun “ways,” rather than an action or description. The word appears in Daniel 4:37 and Daniel 5:23.

This Hebrew word refers to “instruments” that are “musical”—objects used to produce or accompany music. It occurs twice in the Old Testament corpus, both times in Ecclesiastes 2:8. The word therefore names musical equipment rather than an action, person, or feeling. Its normal sense is broad enough to identify instruments collectively, without specifying one particular kind. The surrounding wording connects it with the organized abundance and pleasures described in that passage.

e.t: Ashbel is a personal name, referring to a descendant of Benjamin. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears three times, each time as “Ashbel.” The name occurs in genealogical lists connected with Jacob’s family and Benjamin’s descendants. Because it is a proper name rather than a descriptive term, these passages use it to identify a particular person within Israel’s family records, not to express a general quality or action.

This Hebrew word means “three,” expressing the number that comes after two and before four. It functions as a number word in the Old Testament, describing a count or quantity. It appears 431 times across 381 Old Testament verses, showing regular use whenever Scripture identifies three people, objects, units, or periods. Its meaning remains simple and consistent, while the surrounding passage determines what is being counted.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “power,” referring to the ability or authority held by someone who can command or act with force. In its two Old Testament occurrences, it is connected with a king’s power and with the power from which a person cannot escape. It therefore points to effective authority or control, rather than merely physical strength. The word appears in Ecclesiastes 8:4 and 8:8, both within the same chapter’s reflection on human rule and limitation.

This word refers to a name—the identifying designation by which a person or people are known. It is used in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, especially in Ezra and Daniel, and appears 12 times across 10 verses. Its normal function is to identify or specify someone by name, rather than describe an action or quality. The surrounding wording determines whose name is being mentioned in each passage.

e.t: Shimeam is a personal name, not a common word with a separately stated meaning. It identifies one individual in the Hebrew Old Testament and appears only once, in 1 Chronicles 9:38. Its use belongs to a genealogical record, where names identify people and their place within a family line. The English rendering is “Shimeam,” preserving the name rather than translating it into an ordinary descriptive term. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its specific place in that genealogy.

This Hebrew word means “present.” It names something that is presented or brought to someone, functioning in these passages as the object connected with an action. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in Psalm 72:10 and once in Ezekiel 27:15. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise force in each passage must be read from its context.

e.t: This Hebrew word describes what is false or lying—something untrue rather than trustworthy. It can characterize speech, testimony, or claims that misrepresent reality, and it may also describe conduct marked by falsehood. The word occurs 113 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a broad use in warnings about deceptive speech and unreliable claims. Its normal sense is therefore falsehood expressed in words or actions, with the surrounding sentence showing how the deceit is being presented.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “pillars,” meaning upright supports or structures. It appears twice in the Old Testament, once in Song of Solomon and once in Joel. As a noun, it identifies visible upright forms rather than an action or quality. Its occurrence in Joel is connected with something being given or presented, while its occurrence in Song uses the same basic sense. The surrounding verse supplies the specific picture, but the word itself points to pillars as upright structural forms.

In the Hebrew Bible corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Joshua 18:27. The available rendering preserves the name rather than translating it into an English meaning, so its precise historical or contextual significance must come from the surrounding passage.
